title: URL Parameter Parsing: Plus Signs, Duplicate Keys, Relative URLs
description: A guide to query-string splitting, plus vs. percent decoding, duplicate-key order, relative-URL errors, WHATWG normalization, and the tool's limits.
content:
Parsing URL parameters means splitting the query string after the question mark into key-value pairs on &, then percent-decoding every key and value. Browser and Node WHATWG implementations both use URL and URLSearchParams for this step, and duplicate keys, plus signs, and invalid escapes all behave in fixed ways. The URL parameter parser on this site shows nine address fields (protocol, hostname, port, pathname, search, hash, username, password, and href) plus one row per parameter, so every behavior described below can be reproduced there.

Split the query string into pairs before decoding

The query part starts at the first ? and ends at # or the end of the string; everything after # is the fragment, not a parameter. Parsing first cuts the string on & into segments and drops empty segments. For each segment, the content before the first = is the key and the content after it is the value. The second and later = signs stay in the value, so ?token=abc=def has the key token and the value abc=def, not three fields.

A segment with no equals sign is treated as "key plus empty value": ?flag and ?flag= are both a single record in the parameter table, with an empty string as the value. A semicolon is not a separator, so ?a=1;b=2 yields only one key, a, whose value is 1;b=2. Consecutive empty segments do not create empty records either: ?a=1&&b=2& still has just two parameters, in the same order as the original string.

const u = new URL('https://example.com/path?q=clover&lang=zh-CN&page=2');
for (const [key, value] of u.searchParams) {
  console.log(key, JSON.stringify(value));
}
// q "clover"
// lang "zh-CN"
// page "2"

That loop is the most reliable way to read parameters: searchParams keeps insertion order, and duplicate keys are not overwritten. Converting to a plain object is only safe when you know the keys are unique.

Plus signs and percent encoding are two different decoding rules

In a query string, + decodes to a space under form-encoding rules, %20 also decodes to a space, and a literal plus sign must be written as %2B. So ?q=a+b and ?q=a%20b both produce the value a b, while ?q=a%2Bb produces a+b. The same applies to Chinese text: %E4%B8%AD decodes to the character “中”, and when you enter that character directly, the parser serializes it as %E4%B8%AD; both forms display identically in the parameter table.

This rule comes from the form-encoding parser used by URLSearchParams; do not apply it to decodeURIComponent. decodeURIComponent('a+b') still returns a+b, because it only handles percent escapes. For the same reason, do not use decodeURIComponent on a whole query string: plus signs would remain, and nothing would split the key-value boundaries. If you must process a single value manually, first split on & and =, then replace + with a space, and decode last.

Invalid escapes in a query string do not make parsing fail. For ?a=%zz, search remains ?a=%zz, and reading the value yields the string %zz; incomplete sequences such as %2 are also preserved as-is; and %FF is not valid UTF-8, so decoding produces the replacement character U+FFFD. Invalid percent signs in the path are preserved too, whereas decodeURIComponent('%zz') throws URIError: URI malformed. If parameter values come from outside, do not assume they can always be decoded strictly. When you need to re-encode parameters, use the site's URL encoder; read the original text first so you do not encode an already-encoded %25 a second time.

Duplicate keys and empty values: listed one by one, never grouped

?a=1&a=2 appears as two rows in the tool, both with the key a and with values 1 and 2 respectively. The parser does not merge them into an array and does not let the later value overwrite the earlier one; it simply preserves order of appearance. The single-value accessor get('a') returns the first 1, and you need getAll('a') to get everything. The status bar's "N query parameters" counter counts records, so a duplicate key is counted twice.

Out-of-order duplicates keep their original order too: the three records in ?a=1&b=2&a=3 are a=1, b=2, and a=3 in that sequence. This matters when you debug signatures, pagination, and analytics parameters: if the server reads only the first key, later values with the same name may be silently ignored; if the server builds its own array, its result will not match the two rows you see.

Empty values need to be traced back to their source. ?a= and ?flag both show an empty value in the parameter table, but the "Query" row shows ?a= and ?flag respectively. If the parameters are serialized again, flag is padded to flag=; in other words, the serialized string is not necessarily character-for-character identical to what the user typed. To test whether a parameter exists but is empty, has() is more reliable than checking whether the value is truthy.

The nine fields of the sample address

Parsing the tool's built-in sample address https://user:pass@example.com:8080/path/to/page?q=clover&lang=zh-CN&page=2#section-a yields the nine field values below. This table is also the reference baseline for checking other addresses: when the port, query, hash, username, or password is empty, the tool shows "(default)" or "(none)".

FieldSample valueWhen empty
Protocolhttps:Always present
Hostnameexample.comAlways present
Port8080Shows "(default)"
Path/path/to/pageShows /
Query?q=clover&lang=zh-CN&page=2Shows "(none)"
Hash#section-aShows "(none)"
UsernameuserShows "(none)"
PasswordpassShows "(none)"
Full URLSame as the input—

The three parameters are q=clover, lang=zh-CN, and page=2; the parameter table lists them one by one in the same order as the query string. Note that "Full URL" is the parsed href, not the original input: if the original string contains an uppercase scheme, a default port, or a .. path, this row shows the normalized result.

Normalization rewrites the original string, so do not treat it as the source

new URL() is not a validator; it is a parse-then-serialize process. The scheme and hostname are lowercased, so HTTPS://EXAMPLE.COM/Path becomes https://example.com/Path, while the path's case is preserved. Default ports are removed: https://example.com:443/a has an empty port, and so does http://example.com:80/a; a non-default port such as 8443 is kept. The .. and . segments in a path are collapsed: /a/../b/./c becomes /b/c, and /a/b/.. becomes /a/.

Backslashes are treated as slashes for special schemes: https://example.com/a\b\c has the path /a/b/c. Tabs and newlines are removed, so a tab between /a and b makes the path /ab, not a path containing whitespace. Chinese domain names go through IDNA conversion: https://例子.测试/path reports the hostname xn--fsqu00a.xn--0zwm56d. With no path after the host, a / is added, so https://example.com has the path /. Spaces in the path, query, and hash are all encoded as %20, and the raw character does not remain in href.

One more easily overlooked detail: for https://example.com/?, the href keeps the trailing question mark, but search is an empty string, so the tool's "Query" row shows "(none)". So an address containing a question mark does not necessarily have query parameters; count them from the parameter table.

Why the "Query" row and the parameter table disagree

The "Query" row takes u.search, the serialized query string, which keeps percent encoding; the parameter table takes searchParams.entries(), whose keys and values are already decoded. For example, with ?q=a%26b&x=1 the "Query" row shows ?q=a%26b&x=1, while the parameter table shows a&b as the value of q; for ?q=a%3Db the value displays as a=b. Do not be surprised by a & or = inside the table: that is just a decoded value, not a new separator.

The two sides also encode spaces differently. MDN notes that URL.search encodes a space as %20, while URLSearchParams serializes a space as +. The tool only reads, so it never triggers this rewrite; but if your own code calls set() or append() on searchParams, the URL's search is replaced wholesale, an existing %20 may become +, and the encoding range of other characters may change as well. Before copying the "Full URL", confirm that it has the form you want.

Boundaries and limitations

Before using the tool as a "parameter decoder", review these boundaries. They are not defects; they are the result of a parser that only parses and makes no business judgments.

  • Relative addresses are not supported. The tool calls new URL(raw) without a second base argument, so /path?x=1, example.com/?x=1, //example.com/?x=1, and ?a=1 all throw TypeError: Invalid URL, and the UI says a protocol is required. A relative reference needs a base address to resolve, and supplying one is the caller's responsibility.
  • Normalization rewrites the original string. Default ports disappear, .. path segments collapse, case is unified, Chinese domains become punycode, and tabs are removed; all of this means "Full URL" cannot serve as an audit copy. When you need a character-for-character comparison, keep the input string yourself.
  • Duplicate keys are not grouped. Keys with the same name are listed in order of appearance, without merging, overwriting, or sorting; use getAll for the full set, because a single-value read returns only the first entry.
  • Plus signs and %20 have different meanings. In a query string, + decodes to a space, and a literal plus must be written %2B; decodeURIComponent does not replace +, so the two must not be mixed up.
  • Invalid percent signs and very long parameters do not raise errors. In the query string and path, %zz, %2, and %FF never make parsing fail; values may be preserved as-is or become the replacement character. Runtime logs show that values of twenty thousand characters and five hundred key-value pairs can still be parsed completely, but the tool UI, logging systems, and backend frameworks usually impose their own length and count limits, so the business layer must set caps itself.
  • Nested parameters are not expanded. The key of a[b]=1 is simply the string a[b], never split into an object; data={...} is just a string too, and the tool does not parse JSON. To read a JSON value, extract the string first and process it with the JSONPath query tool or a JSON formatter.
  • Business meaning is not validated. Required fields, types, signatures, permissions, and duplicate submissions are outside the parser's scope; successful parsing only means the format was accepted by the URL parser.
  • Only the query string is considered. #a=2 in the fragment is not a parameter; usernames and passwords are displayed in plain text, so do not paste addresses containing real tokens, phone numbers, or passwords into any online tool.

Put it into code: a four-item checklist

Turning the behaviors above into a fixed order of checks prevents most "it looks right locally but the value is missing in production" problems.

  1. Iterate entries() rather than using Object.fromEntries. The former preserves order and duplicate keys; the latter leaves only the last value for each name.
  2. Use get for a single value, getAll for multiple values, and has for presence; do not use truthiness to distinguish an empty value from a missing one.
  3. Do not decode a value that URLSearchParams already decoded; decoding %2520 a second time yields a space and corrupts the original data.
  4. If you need the original query string, keep the input or read search; do not reconstruct it from href. Perform business validation separately after parsing.

If a URL is buried in logs, documents, or chat history, first extract the addresses with the regex tester, then check them one by one in the parser; that is more reliable than counting & by hand. When you need to generate or rewrite parameters, process each key and value with the URL encoder and then reassemble the query string, which avoids ambiguity around plus signs and spaces.

faqs.a: Because the call to new URL(raw) does not pass a second base argument, and /path is a relative reference; both browser and Node WHATWG implementations throw TypeError: Invalid URL. The tool therefore says a protocol is required. Add an https://example.com prefix or pass a base to parse it.

faqs.q: Why does ?a=1&a=2 show two rows but reading the value return only 1?
faqs.a: URLSearchParams keeps duplicate keys as two records: the table lists them one by one, and get('a') returns the first 1; use getAll('a') to retrieve all of them, in the same order as the query string. The tool does not merge them into an array.

faqs.q: Why does a plus sign in a parameter turn into a space?
faqs.a: URLSearchParams parses according to application/x-www-form-urlencoded, so + decodes to a space; %2B is the literal plus sign. Calling decodeURIComponent on the whole string does not convert +, and it throws URIError on %zz.

faqs.q: Chinese parameters display as Chinese, but the Query row still shows %E4%B8%AD?
faqs.a: The parameter table shows decoded keys and values; the Query row is u.search, the query string with percent encoding preserved. One is a decoded view, the other is the serialization result; look at the Query row when you need the original encoding.

focus: Split on & first, cut each pair at the first =, then decode as UTF-8; keep duplicate keys as separate records.
notice: Parsing runs locally in your browser, so the URL is never uploaded. Do not paste addresses containing account credentials or tokens into any online tool.
